title: The Dynamic-Probabilistic Consistency Gap in Chaotic Surrogate Modeling
claim: Common training objectives each break either the learned dynamics or the uncertainty's link to them; ours keeps both consistent.
layout: 4 columns, left-to-right, three failure panels then ours, color-coded headers
description: Four equal columns are separated by thin vertical rules. Each has a colored top bar and bold colored title: orange 'Core collapse', blue 'Noise masking', pink 'Blind uncertainty' and green 'KAFFEE'. Each column shows a grey Lorenz-attractor butterfly as ground truth, with a learned trajectory overlaid in the column's color. In core collapse the orange curve spirals inward to a point. In noise masking a small blue loop sits inside a large translucent blue uncertainty blob. In blind uncertainty the pink curve follows the attractor, but its small circles are scattered and unrelated to the local dynamics. In KAFFEE the green curve follows the attractor and thin ellipses stretch along it. Below each is a one-line takeaway in black, then two grey lines naming the objective and whether Jacobian propagation is used. The eye goes first to the colored titles and the differing curves.
caption: The DPC gap in probabilistic DSR. Schematic comparison of three DPC failure modes and KAFFEE. Finite-horizon probabilistic scores can improve while autonomous dynamics deteriorate or uncertainty remains blind to local dynamics. KAFFEE pairs filtered innovation scoring with Jacobian-based covariance propagation to mitigate the DPC gap. Grey curves illustrate ground-truth dynamics, colored curves learned autonomous dynamics, and shading learned predictive uncertainty.
abstract: Dynamical systems reconstruction (DSR) aims to learn surrogate models that capture the dynamics underlying time-series data. Reliable scientific inference with these surrogates requires uncertainty estimates consistent with the learned dynamics. We expose a dynamic-probabilistic consistency (DPC) gap: optimizing finite-horizon probabilistic objectives can degrade the learned dynamics or decouple predictive uncertainty from the local tangent dynamics it should reflect. We isolate three mechanisms behind this gap: core collapse, noise masking, and blind uncertainty. Specifically, we show that open-loop rollout objectives can penalize covariance growth driven by the dynamics, encouraging optimization shortcuts that weaken local expansion. To mitigate this gap, we propose KAFFEE (Kalman-Aware Framework For Ergodic Emulation), a differentiable extended Kalman filter-based training framework that jointly learns dynamics and noise covariances by coupling filtered innovation likelihoods with covariance propagation through learned local Jacobians, while differentiating through the Kalman updates. On stochastic hyperchaotic Lorenz-96, KAFFEE mitigates the identified failure modes and improves both reconstruction of dynamical invariants and predictive scores relative to open-loop objectives. The DPC gap also appears when probabilistically adapting a DSR foundation model across 13 chaotic systems, where KAFFEE improves predictive likelihood over open-loop adaptation while preserving the pretrained model's long-term dynamics and enabling in-context Bayesian filtering.
